analysis.one_liner: Blocks states from adopting rules that phase out the sale of new gas-powered cars.
analysis.headline: The bill never left committee and never got a vote; its 17 Senate supporters were all Republicans.
analysis.plain_summary: Under current law, states like California can set their own vehicle emissions rules if the EPA grants them a waiver. This bill would change the Clean Air Act so that no state standard could limit the sale or use of new gas-powered cars in any way, direct or indirect. It would also force the EPA to take back any waivers granted since January 2022 that have that effect, unwinding rules already in place, such as California's requirement that a rising share of new cars sold be electric [S2][S3]. The bill was introduced in June 2023 and referred to the Senate Environment and Public Works Committee, which took no action before the Congress ended [S1][S5].
analysis.who_benefits: Consumers who want to keep buying new gasoline-powered cars would keep that option guaranteed in federal law, since no state could adopt a rule phasing them out. Oil and gas producers would benefit from gasoline demand staying stronger for longer, and automakers and dealers would avoid the cost of meeting state-mandated electric-vehicle sales targets [S2][S3].
analysis.who_benefits_short: Gas-car buyers, oil producers, car dealers

how_it_helps.text: The bill amends the Clean Air Act so the EPA may not grant a waiver for any state vehicle standard that directly or indirectly limits the sale or use of new internal-combustion-engine vehicles, keeping the choice to buy a new gas car open nationwide [S2][S3].
It requires the EPA to revoke any waiver granted between January 1, 2022 and enactment that has that effect, unwinding state rules already adopted during that window [S2][S3].
It also bars the EPA from treating state standards amended after enactment as covered by existing waivers, closing off a path states had used to tighten their rules without a fresh waiver [S2][S3].

analysis.who_pays: The cost would fall on states' ability to set stricter air-quality rules: state electric-vehicle sales mandates would become impossible, and the pace of switching away from gasoline vehicles would slow. That means more tailpipe pollution and greenhouse gas emissions over time, and households in states that wanted the transition would not get it. Electric-vehicle makers and charging companies would lose a government-guaranteed sales pipeline [S2][S3].

drawbacks.text: Blocking state rules that limit gas-car sales would leave more conventional tailpipe pollution and greenhouse gas emissions on the road for longer, since the bill removes the main legal tool states used to push the vehicle fleet toward zero-emission cars [S2][S3].

The bill reaches beyond outright bans: it disqualifies any standard that 'directly or indirectly' limits the sale or use of gas vehicles, a broad standard that could sweep in ordinary emissions rules that make gas cars costlier to certify, taking away far more state authority than the headline 'no ban' framing suggests [S3].

Supporters' choice argument cuts both ways: guaranteeing the right to buy a gas car also guarantees that buyers who want an EV-lean market, cleaner air, or lower fuel costs in states that voted for those rules do not get them [S2].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The genuine benefit is real but narrow: some households prefer gasoline vehicles and would face higher upfront costs under a state EV mandate, and this bill locks in their choice. The cost is broader and longer-lasting: it strips states of their most effective clean-air tool, slows the shift away from gasoline, and does so retroactively for rules adopted since 2022. On balance the bill trades a state-led emissions transition for a federal guarantee of the status quo, and the drafters wrote the 'indirectly' language broadly enough that ordinary state emissions rules could be swept in.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and sent to the Senate Environment and Public Works Committee, which never acted on it, so it died when the Congress ended in January 2025.

narrative.text: Senator Mullin introduced the bill on June 21, 2023, joined by eight other Republican senators as original cosponsors [S3].
Sixteen Republicans in total cosponsored the bill — 16 of the Senate's 49 Republicans — with no Democratic support listed [S4].
The Senate read it twice and referred it to the Committee on Environment and Public Works, and the action history shows no further steps: no hearing, no markup, no floor vote [S5].
The 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025, so the bill expired in committee without ever reaching the Senate floor [S1].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: States that had adopted or planned electric-vehicle sales mandates, along with the emissions reductions those rules were meant to produce, are better off because the bill died. The oil and gas industry did not get the federal guarantee of continued gasoline-vehicle sales it would have gained from the bill, though existing rules still face litigation and future Congresses could take the same approach.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: States' EV mandates and emissions rules survived

for.name: Sen. Markwayne Mullin
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and recruited eight other Republican senators as original cosponsors.

for.name: 16 of 49 Senate Republicans
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill; all listed cosponsors were Republicans.

against.name: Senate Environment and Public Works Committee
against.role: Committee of referral, chaired by a Democrat in the 118th Congress
against.what_they_did: Held the bill after referral; the record shows no hearing, markup, or vote, so it never reached the floor.

against.name: Senate Democratic majority
against.role: Held 48 of 100 Senate seats and controlled the committee calendar
against.what_they_did: Brought no version of the bill to the floor and advanced no vehicle-waiver restriction during the 118th Congress.

sides.party_line_note: Every sponsor and cosponsor was a Republican (16 of 49 Senate Republicans), no Democrat cosponsored, and the Democratic majority that controlled the committee and floor schedule never acted on it.

industries.note: The bill would have protected gasoline demand by making it legally impossible for states to phase out gas-car sales. Its success would have come at the cost of the emissions reductions those state rules were designed to deliver [S2][S3].

Automakers and dealers would avoid the retooling and inventory costs of state EV sales mandates, and dealers in particular benefit from continued gas-car sales. Some major automakers had nonetheless backed the California rules for regulatory certainty, so the benefit was not universal [S2].

State mandates were a guaranteed, growing market for EVs and chargers; the bill would have removed that pipeline and taken back waivers already granted. The industry's loss would have coincided with slower emissions reductions for the public.
